query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloys, the dynamic mechanical response is controlled by a strain rate and temperature–dependent transition between deformation twinning and dislocation slip. The absence of cobalt produces local fluctuations in stacking fault energy that mediate whether dislocation accumulation evolves into twin formation (enhancing work hardening and ductility) or remains dominated by slip (increasing flow stress), thereby maintaining the strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy with a predominantly FCC structure that exhibits nanoscale compositional inhomogeneities.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of strain rate and temperature during mechanical testing.
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tensile or compressive tests conducted over a broad range of strain rates (from quasi-static up to high dynamic rates) and temperatures (from cryogenic to moderately elevated temperatures).
generation.structural_mediator: Local variations in stacking fault energy and minor chemical fluctuations at the nanoscale that act as barriers or promoters for twin nucleation.
generation.mechanism: At lower strain rates and/or lower temperatures, reduced thermal activation favors dislocation pile-up and the nucleation of deformation twins, which increases work hardening and ductility. At higher strain rates and/or elevated temperatures, enhanced dynamic recovery and dislocation mobility suppress twinning, shifting the mechanism toward dislocation slip and producing a distinct change in flow stress and strain hardening behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in twin density and an increase in the proportion of slip-dominated deformation with increasing strain rate and temperature, reflected in shifts in yield strength and work hardening rates, as well as changes in serrated flow behavior in the stress–strain curves.
generation.baseline: At room temperature and moderate strain rate, the FeNiCrMn alloy exhibits a mixed deformation mode with both dislocation slip and a noticeable fraction of deformation twins.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies to as-solidified, Co–free FeNiCrMn alloys with a primarily FCC microstructure; results may vary if significant secondary phases or substantial microstructural refinement due to post-processing are present.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative contributions of twinning versus slip may depend on subtle compositional gradients and processing history. Additionally, other mechanisms (e.g., dynamic recrystallization) might also influence the performance under extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of solidified Co–free FeNiCrMn alloy specimens and perform in situ uniaxial mechanical tests at various strain rates (quasi-static to dynamic) and temperatures (cryogenic to elevated). Utilize high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) during or after deformation to quantify the fractions of deformation twins versus dislocation slip features.
measurements: Stress–strain response (yield strength, work hardening rate)
Quantitative microstructural analysis (twin density, dislocation density)
Serration characteristics of dynamic stress–strain curves
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If experiments reveal no systematic decrease in twin density (or no shift from twin-dominated to slip-dominated mechanisms) with increasing strain rate and temperature, or if changes in stacking fault energy (inferred from local compositional/structural analysis) do not correlate with the measured mechanical response, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Experiments and Model for Serration Statistics in Low-Entropy, Medium-Entropy, and High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new alloys that contain five or more elements in roughly-equal proportion. We present new experiments and theory on the deformation behavior of HEAs under slow stretching (straining), and observe differences, compared to conventional alloys with fewer elements. For a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates, HEAs deform in a jerky way, with sudden slips that make it difficult to precisely control the deformation. An analytic model explains these slips as avalanches of slipping weak spots and predicts the observed slip statistics, stress-strain curves, and their dependence on temperature, strain-rate, and material composition. The ratio of the weak spots’ healing rate to the strain-rate is the main tuning parameter, reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier effect and time-temperature superposition in polymers. Our model predictions agree with the experimental results. The proposed widely-applicable deformation mechanism is useful for deformation control and alloy design.

High-velocity deformation of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy: Remarkable resistance to shear failure

Abstract: The mechanical behavior of a single phase (fcc) Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) was studied in the low and high strain-rate regimes. The combination of multiple strengthening mechanisms such as solid solution hardening, forest dislocation hardening, as well as mechanical twinning leads to a high work hardening rate, which is significantly larger than that for Al and is retained in the dynamic regime. The resistance to shear localization was studied by dynamically-loading hat-shaped specimens to induce forced shear localization. However, no adiabatic shear band could be observed. It is therefore proposed that the excellent strain hardening ability gives rise to remarkable resistance to shear localization, which makes this material an excellent candidate for penetration protection applications such as armors.

Extracting information from noisy data: strain mapping during dynamic in situ SEM experiments

Abstract: AbstractAbstractMicromechanical testing techniques can reveal a variety of characteristics in materials that are otherwise impossible to address. However, unlike to macroscopic testing, these miniaturized experiments are more challenging to realize and analyze, as loading and boundary conditions can often not be controlled to the same extent as in standardized macroscopic tests. Hence, exploiting all possible information from such an experiment seems utmost desirable. In the present work, we utilize dynamic in situ microtensile testing of a nanocrystalline equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy in conjunction with initial feature tracking to obtain a continuous two-dimensional strain field. This enables an evaluation of true stress–strain data as well as of the Poisson’s ratio and allows to study localization of plastic deformation for the specimen.
